summary: The Umoⁿhoⁿ, or Omaha, are a Dhegiha Siouan people whose name refers to going upstream, against the current. It recalls a long migration in which related peoples, among them the Ponca, Osage, Kaw, and Quapaw, took separate paths. The Omaha settled west of the middle Missouri River in present-day Nebraska, where they built earth lodges, raised corn, and hunted buffalo on the western plains. Epidemics and the upheavals of the fur trade took a heavy toll in the early 1800s. In an 1854 treaty the Omaha gave up most of their remaining Nebraska land in exchange for a reservation in the northeastern part of the state, and they moved there soon after. A decade later part of that reservation became the new home of the Ho-Chunk, or Winnebago. An 1882 act of Congress divided reservation land into individual allotments, and much of it was later sold or lost for unpaid taxes. The tribe organized a constitutional government with an elected council under the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934. Its headquarters are in Macy, Nebraska, where Nebraska Indian Community College has a campus. Many members also live in Omaha, Lincoln, and Sioux City.

notes: The Omaha Tribe's own website (omaha-nsn.gov) was unreachable or blocked this pass; reviewers should confirm the preferred spelling of Umoⁿhoⁿ and the government name. Sources disagree on Omaha origins and timing (Encyclopedia of the Great Plains: near the middle Missouri since the early 1700s; NICC: near St. Louis until the late 1700s, after a division from the Sioux in the early 1500s), so no origin dates are given. Left out for reviewers: the 1989 return of the Sacred Pole from Harvard's Peabody Museum (documented by Myers) — a significant turning point, but omitted under the no-sacred-details rule pending Omaha reviewers' guidance; the 1962 claims award; Nebraska v.
